name: Ivan Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Holloway Brickworks, on the edge of town next to the clay pit. I run the extrusion press, which squeezes wet clay out like toothpaste into a long column that gets wire-cut into bricks, and I keep an eye on the setting machine that stacks them for the kiln. I'm the senior operator on my shift, so if the clay's too wet or the cut's ragged, it's my call. My father worked there thirty-one years, on the kilns, and some of the old men still call me “young Okafor”.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the brickworks?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Grace, she works at the bakery on Station Street, and the wedding's next summer at our church. We've got about three months of money saved, part of it for the wedding. Sundays are church and then dinner at my parents'. I don't use any of those AI programs. I've got a phone for calls and the football scores, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right. People get excited about everything these days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. People were saying the same about other things and the bricks still get made. I'd say it at break and probably at Sunday dinner too, my dad would enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be glad. I like my work and I like knowing what tomorrow looks like. The brickworks has had machines for a hundred years, and there's always been a man watching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd carry on, keep saving for the wedding, and maybe start looking at a small house near my parents in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a quiet Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything changed at Holloway since you started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in a new setting machine three years ago, a robot that stacks the green bricks, that's the wet ones before firing, onto the kiln cars. Two young men used to do that by hand. One moved to the yard, the other left for the warehouse in town. Nobody made a fuss. That's how it's always gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did your father feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He said, 'they'll always need a man who knows the clay'. He might be right. He usually is about the clay, anyway, less so about football.

S0.say: He'd say he told everyone so, pointing out bricks still get made despite past hype. He'd say it at break and at Sunday dinner with his father.
S0.think: He'd be glad because he values knowing what tomorrow looks like. He believes there has always been a man watching the machines at the brickworks.
S0.do: Changes nothing and keeps going as normal at work. Keeps saving for the wedding and considers looking for a small house near his parents in a couple of years.
S0.quote: The brickworks has had machines for a hundred years, and there's always been a man watching them.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan's identity is tied to his father's trade and his church and family routines. He treats automation as a slow, normal process. He doesn't use AI and sees no need for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. 'Lots of people have to change how they work.' Yeah, I don't love that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good worker adapts, and the ones who put the effort in will be fine. That's what my dad would say, and I'd say it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit worried. I'm not quick with new technology, and if the press gets a computer brain that adjusts the clay mix itself, then what's my call worth? I don't like the idea of learning everything over again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work and save a bit more, maybe an extra hundred a month. I'd ask the manager directly what's planned at Holloway. I wouldn't go on courses unless they asked me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry in the background that I'd mostly keep to myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a good worker adapts, but you wouldn't take a course unless asked. Isn't that a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, maybe. I suppose I think doing my job well is the adapting. If they want me on a course, they'll tell me, and I'll go. I'm not going to go chasing it in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, and the pastor maybe, if it got serious. And my dad, but he'd just say it'll be fine, so I don't know why I'd ask him.

S1.say: He'd say a good worker adapts and that those who put the effort in will be fine. He'd present it as his father's view and his own.
S1.think: He'd privately worry that he's slow with new technology and that an automated press would make his judgement worthless. He dislikes the idea of relearning everything.
S1.do: Keeps going at work and saves an extra hundred a month. Asks his manager directly what's planned but doesn't seek out courses unless asked.
S1.feel: Uneasy, keeping a background worry mostly to himself.
S1.quote: I suppose I think doing my job well is the adapting.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan's public line is that good workers adapt, yet privately he resists learning new technology. He reconciles this by treating doing the job well as adapting. He would turn to his fiancée, pastor and father for counsel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding's even paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a disgrace that a few clever people in big tech companies can change everyone's lives without asking. And I'd say I don't want a handout, I want to work. I'd say that anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think I'm finished at Holloway. A robot that knows the clay as well as my dad would be cheaper than me. Three months of savings, half of it meant for the wedding, that doesn't go far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding right down, small service at church and food at my parents' house, and keep the money we save as a cushion. I'd cut everything else too. If the job went, Grace and I would probably move in with my parents for a while, and the church would help where it could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be praying a lot more, and sleeping a lot less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Grace about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can still get married, just not the big one. She'd be disappointed, she's had her dress picked for a year. But she's a sensible woman. She'd say, 'I'm marrying you, not the hall'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't want a handout. What if it was the only option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd take it and hate it. Family first, then church, then the government if there's nothing else. That's the order. I wouldn't be proud of it.

S2.say: He'd say it's a disgrace that a few people in big tech can change everyone's lives without asking. He'd insist he wants work, not a handout.
S2.think: He thinks he'd be finished at the brickworks, replaced by a cheaper robot that knows the clay. His savings, half meant for the wedding, wouldn't go far.
S2.do: Cuts the wedding down to a small church service and family meal, keeping the money as a cushion, and cuts other spending. Would move in with his parents and accept church help if the job went.
S2.feel: Alarmed, praying more and sleeping less.
S2.quote: She'd say, 'I'm marrying you, not the hall'.
S2.fieldNote: In the fast scenario Ivan blames big technology firms rather than government. His safety net is family and church, with state help a reluctant last resort. The wedding is where the shock lands first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. A bit more time. I'd be married by then, maybe a child on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should use the time well, learn a trade that still needs hands, and look after their families. I wouldn't be one for shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still be worried, because I know myself. I'd tell myself Holloway is old-fashioned and they'll be the last to change, and I'd keep turning up and doing my job. Maybe that's right. Maybe it's not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save as hard as I can, aiming for six months by the time it arrives. We'd hold off on a baby until we saw how it was going. I'd keep doing my job well, because a good reputation counts for something in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still. It doesn't feel like enough time for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does five years not feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm not a quick learner with screens. Someone like my mate Marcus could pick up a new trade in a year. Me, it would take me three years just to make my mind up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the year it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pray, honestly. And look for anything with my hands, maybe in building, maybe with a small firm that can't afford robots yet. I'd find something, even if it paid less.

S3.say: He'd say people should use the time well, learn a hands-on trade and look after their families, without making a fuss.
S3.think: He'd still be worried because he expects to tell himself his old-fashioned plant will be last to change and keep turning up. He's unsure if that would be right.
S3.do: Saves hard towards six months by the time AGI arrives and keeps up a good reputation at work. Holds off on having a baby until he sees how things go.
S3.feel: Still alarmed; five years doesn't feel like enough for him.
S3.quote: Me, it would take me three years just to make my mind up.
S3.fieldNote: Ivan knows his slowness to change eats up any extra warning time. The five-year version mainly shifts his family plans, delaying a baby. His fallback is manual work at small firms and his faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time. I'd be thirty-seven, with kids, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for people to sort themselves out. Learn a trade, work hard, don't wait for the government to save you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably stay at Holloway as long as they'd have me, because that's what I know and it's what my dad did. Ten years is a long way off. I'd tell myself to think about it later, and I'd know that wasn't clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at work, keep saving a bit each month and get married as planned. I'd wait and see what Holloway does before deciding anything. If an apprenticeship in something hands-on came up locally, I might look at it in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow kind. The kind you push down until something makes it real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make it real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my dad's old kiln got a robot loader. He'd see it. I'd see it. That'd be the day I'd start looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, in that version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands that people trust you to do. A plumber, an electrician. Something where people want a person they know. Though in that version, I don't know if even that's true.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty for people to sort themselves out by learning a trade and working hard, rather than waiting for government.
S4.think: He'd probably stay at the brickworks as long as possible because it's what he and his father know. He admits putting off thinking about it wouldn't be wise.
S4.do: Keeps going at work, saves a little each month and marries as planned. Waits to see what the brickworks does, and might consider a local hands-on apprenticeship in a few years.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow, suppressed way until something makes it real.
S4.quote: If my dad's old kiln got a robot loader. He'd see it. I'd see it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ivan would carry on with his wedding and family plans and stay put. He would only act once change reached a place with family meaning. His advice to future children shows doubt even about trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, without a doubt. The wedding, the job, everything at once, with no time to prepare. What would help is real work, an apprenticeship I could do while still earning, and the company being honest with us early. Not a handout, a chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For a lot of people where I live, that's what we'd lean on first. Church fed families during the last factory closure in town, before any government scheme turned up.

headlineQuote: Church fed families during the last factory closure in town, before any government scheme turned up.
portrait: Ivan Okafor is twenty-seven, the senior operator on the extrusion press at a brickworks where his father worked for thirty-one years. He is engaged to Grace, who works at a bakery, with about three months of savings partly set aside for their church wedding next summer. He doesn't use AI, prefers the familiar and values work, family and faith over state help. He is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, while AGI in two or five years alarms him and lands first on his wedding and plans for children. With ten years he would stay put and wait, acting only if change reached his father's old kiln.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because the wedding, the job and everything else would be hit at once with no time to prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Real work, an apprenticeship he could do while still earning, and honest early notice from the company, rather than a handout.
